name: Leg press
angleNote: Knee flexion: 10° = legs nearly straight, 110° = sled lowered deep. Lifting makes the angle smaller. Torques are per leg; drag the figure to turn it.
momentArmNote: Moment arm = the joint's 3D distance from the plate's push line; it feeds every component of that joint's torque.

strength.note: Relative isometric hip-extension torque vs hip flexion, peak about 53°, measured standing with the knee slightly bent (tested −29° to 74°; deeper hip flexion is held flat at the 74° value, which is extrapolation). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Relative isometric knee-extension torque vs knee flexion: weakest near full extension, peak about 65° (Anderson, tested 0–103°). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Lindahl et al. found the same shape (peak near 50°, about 50% of peak at 10°). Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022; Lindahl O, Movin A, Ringqvist I (1969/1972). Isometric knee extension strength as a function of joint angle, muscle length and motor unit activity. Acta Orthop Scand 43:138–147

negative.note: Knee flexion (negative torque: hamstrings and gastrocnemius pull the knee back). Anderson et al.'s knee-flexion curve and peak, as in the leg curl, measured seated with the hip at about 70°; corrected for the hip angle below.
negative.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Relative isometric plantarflexion torque vs plantarflexion (negative = dorsiflexed), peak about 23° of dorsiflexion, measured with the knee bent 50° (tested 29° dorsiflexion to 34° plantarflexion). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Hip adductor (positive) and abductor (negative) peak torque per leg, taken as constant across the range: Welsh et al.'s isometric means at 10° of hip abduction (trained recreational hockey players, hip straight): adductors 247 Nm, abductors 130 Nm. Abductor strength falls as the hip abducts (Neumann et al.; Welsh et al.), which isn't modelled here.
strength.source: Welsh P, Howitt S, Howarth SJ (2020). The influence of hip joint angle on the ratio between adduction and abduction torque in experienced, recreational male ice hockey players. Int J Sports Phys Ther 15(1):22–33. doi:10.26603/ijspt20200022

strength.note: Hip external (positive) and internal (negative) rotation peak torque per leg, taken as constant; the external side includes the gluteus maximus. Approximate.
strength.source: TODO: rotation torques not taken from a source yet (Kulig et al. 1984 review only the curve shapes: internal rotation ascending, external descending)

strength.note: No muscle capacity: a sideways knee moment is carried mostly by ligaments and the joint surfaces, so it is shown as torque only.
strength.source: Not applicable: carried by ligaments and joint surfaces, so no muscle strength is used

ankle.note: Two-joint gastrocnemius: plantarflexion strength by knee flexion, relative to the base curve's test at 50° (Cresswell et al., Table 1: 134.9 Nm straight, 103.7 Nm at 90°, 80.4 Nm at 120°). A straight knee makes the calves about 20% stronger, a deep knee bend about 28% weaker.
ankle.source: Cresswell AG, Löscher WN, Thorstensson A (1995). Influence of gastrocnemius muscle length on triceps surae torque development and electromyographic activity in man. Exp Brain Res 105:283–290 (Table 1: 10 men, isometric, ankle 5° dorsiflexed)

knee.note: Two-joint hamstrings: knee-flexion strength by hip flexion, relative to the base curve's test at about 70° (Guex et al.: 62 Nm with the hip straight, 110 Nm at 90°, knee at 45°). Measured at one knee angle only.
knee.source: Guex K, Gojanovic B, Millet GP (2012). Influence of hip-flexion angle on hamstrings isokinetic activity in sprinters. J Athl Train 47(4):390–395. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-47.4.04 (Table: isometric, knee at 45°, 10 sprinters)

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.note: All four heads extend the knee, so net joint torques can't say how the toe angle shifts work between vastus medialis and lateralis.

muscles.name: Gluteus maximus
muscles.note: Main hip extensor; deep hip bend (feet high) loads it more.

muscles.name: Adductor magnus
muscles.note: Rear part extends the hip, more so when it is deeply bent.

muscles.name: Adductors (longus, brevis, gracilis)
muscles.note: Work when the plate's push tends to spread the thighs apart: wide stances and toes out.

muscles.name: Gluteus medius and minimus
muscles.note: Work when the push tends to pull the thighs together: narrow stances, toes in.

muscles.name: Deep hip external rotators
muscles.note: Piriformis, obturators and gemelli (with the glutes) resist the thigh turning inwards.

muscles.name: Calves (soleus, gastrocnemius)
muscles.note: Plantarflexors: push through the ball of the foot.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Legs nearly straight: the push line passes close to the knees.

phases.name: Bottom
phases.text: Deep: the knees and hips have their largest moment arms.

variants.name: Feet middle, shoulder width
variants.notes: The plate pushes along the rail through the middle of each foot. Each joint's torque depends on how far it sits from that push line, in 3D. Sled weight and friction are ignored, and the plate is assumed to push straight (no sideways grip).

variants.name: Feet high
variants.notes: Feet higher on the plate: the push line passes further from the hip and closer to the knee. More hip work, less knee work.

variants.name: Feet low
variants.notes: Feet low on the plate: the push line passes close to (or below) the hip and far from the knee. Mostly knee work, and the ankle bends further.

variants.name: Wide stance, toes out 30°
variants.notes: Feet wide and turned out, knees over the toes. The push now tends to spread the thighs apart and turn them inwards, so the adductors and the hip's external rotators have to hold against it.

variants.name: Narrow stance, toes forward
variants.notes: Feet under the hips: almost everything stays in the side-view plane, so the sideways and rotation torques nearly vanish.

variants.name: Toes in 10°
variants.notes: Turning the toes in (with the knees following them) brings the knees towards each other.

variants.name: Knees caving in
variants.notes: Same foot position as the middle preset, but the knees drift 10° inside the line over the toes: the knee's sideways (valgus) moment rises, which ligaments rather than muscles have to carry.
